name: Marco Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior operator feeding rubber compound into an extruder that makes sealing strips for windows. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead to check my temperature setting. I like seeing a smooth roll come through; a wet batch makes bubbles and a long cleanup.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are work, home and AI use for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner visits older people as a home-care worker, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn typical factory pay, we have about four months of expenses saved and some similar plants nearby. I use AI now and then to understand fault messages, but check the manual and machine before changing a setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the rubber-seal crew AI can tidy the production notes if it wants. The extrusion line still needs somebody to check the seal's width and cut out a bubble before a roll goes to a builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My operator pay is typical, my partner has regular home-care shifts, and we have about four months of expenses saved. There are some similar plants nearby. A modest change leaves me time to become quicker at the line without risking the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep feeding the extruder and measuring the first seal from each new batch with the lead. I already use AI now and then to decipher a fault message, then check the manual before touching a control. We'll keep putting a new amount from each full pay month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a small tool in a working factory, and I still have a wage and a machine to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was the fault explanation wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the AI explanation blamed a heater, but the lead found wet rubber feed. We dried the wet rubber and made a clean sealing strip before shipping the roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner visits older people at home, and our two children are in school. We use the four-month reserve for actual gaps, not for guessing at a machine that might arrive years from now.

say: **AI notes** can be faster while real seals still need width and bubble checks.
The **rubber line** must make a clean strip before shipping.
think: Two regular **household wages** and four months saved feel secure now.
Some nearby **plant jobs** add options if the extrusion line changes.
do: **Keep** feeding and measuring rubber seals with the lead operator each shift.
**Add** new savings from full monthly wages.
feel: **Calm** about paid factory work under modest AI change.
S0.quote: We dried the wet rubber and made a clean sealing strip before shipping the roll.
fieldNote: Marco already uses **AI occasionally** for fault words and checks the manual and actual feed.
The **moderate reserve** and stable household work support calm while he learns extrusion.

steps.text: Keep feeding rubber extruder and measuring first seals
Add new money from full factory wages to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI may change the orders and cut lists before a robot can touch our hot rubber. The union should get paid time for checking new recipes, because a bad setting can waste a whole roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect my own shifts to fall just because the office buys faster. My partner's home-care work is hands-on too, so our two wages look fairly steady. I would learn a proved AI recipe screen after another line has tested it safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union shift steward for paid checking time. If the company offers a supervised paid lesson on its new AI recipe controls, I'll learn to correct a batch on an idle extruder and compare five rolls with the approved measurements. Until a place is offered, I'll keep the current settings and written checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about rushing hot material through a new plan, although our own paid hours look safe for now. I want proof on real rubber, not a colourful dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare the first five rolls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check width, hardness and the first metre for bubbles, then record which change the new screen recommended. If it fails those checks, the old recipe stays in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a recipe lesson safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lesson needs a cooled, stopped machine and the lead beside me; I won't experiment with a live die. I am requesting a place, not saying the lesson has been booked.

say: **AI ordering** may change before robots reach hot-rubber extrusion.
The union should protect **paid checking time** for new recipes.
think: Our own **paid hours** appear secure in this slower change.
A **proved recipe screen** is worth learning in a safe paid lesson.
do: **Ask** union steward for paid recipe checking time.
**Learn** AI recipe correction if supervised paid place offered.
**Keep** approved settings until five rolls pass inspection.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed production while household pay remains stable.
S1.quote: I want proof on real rubber, not a colourful dashboard.
fieldNote: The **paid lesson is requested**, with actual participation conditional on an offered stopped-machine slot.
He would **learn new controls** beyond his existing occasional fault-code checks once another line proves them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028 may plan rubber orders, then capable robots around 2031 could feed, set and inspect an extrusion line. I'd tell our union we need a paid route into maintenance before the line crew is reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the physical robots arrive. Four months saved and some nearby plants give us choices, but a lost typical wage would still strain the mortgage and two children. My partner's home-care shifts might last longer, but I cannot ask one wage to carry everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union steward for a written crew timetable and request a funded, paid-time extruder-maintenance course with guarded practice. If the plant offers a real recognized place, I'll attend. After qualifying, if my shifts fall, I'll apply for posted local machine-maintenance roles only if safe duties, regular hours and pay cover our bills; if no course opens, I'll apply for posted local extrusion work at enough pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a realistic cut to my own shifts, though I can act before the reserve runs down. Learning a safe repair beats waiting for an alarm to replace me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe maintenance practice include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have to isolate the heater and prove the die has cooled before reaching inside. The instructor should make us practise on a stopped machine with the guard in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a maintenance post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the advertised base rate and hours with our mortgage, food and transport. A maintenance title with lower take-home pay would not solve the problem.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes ordering before robots run extrusion around 2031.
The union should obtain **paid maintenance places** before crew cuts.
think: At **48**, losing a typical operator wage would strain our mortgage.
Four months of **savings** and some local plants offer time, not a guarantee.
do: **Request** written crew timing and funded paid maintenance training.
**Attend** recognized guarded course if an actual paid place opens.
**Apply** for posted safe local maintenance after qualifying if shifts fall and pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about possible own paid-hour loss, with several options.
S2.quote: A maintenance title with lower take-home pay would not solve the problem.
fieldNote: He separates a **course request** from real conditional paid enrolment and a later qualified application.
The **fallback extrusion search** requires no paid course, reduced hours and sufficient local wages.

steps.text: Ask union steward for crew timetable and paid maintenance places
Attend recognized extruder course if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply for posted safe local maintenance if qualified, shifts cut, pay sufficient
Apply for posted local extrusion work if no course, shifts cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI reaches orders in 2031 and capable robots run the extruders around 2034, I'd tell the line that five years is enough to prove a maintenance path. The union still has to make training paid, not just available after shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when hands-on robots reach us. My children would be older, but our mortgage may still need two wages. The longer lead gives me time to qualify while drawing my current pay, if the company offers a proper place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep running the extrusion line and save new money from each full month after the household bills. If the plant offers a recognized maintenance certificate with paid release and guarded practice, I'll enrol next year. If my line hours later fall and I qualify, I'll apply to posted local maintenance jobs with safe duties and base pay and hours that cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage in 2034, though not as rushed as the fast case. I can learn a second role without giving up the wage that pays the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real assessment cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to practise a blocked die, a heater fault and the emergency stop with the lead watching. A factory maintenance course should end with a real machine assessment, not a sales demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a local posting state?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting must show a base wage and a safe shift pattern, not only an overtime estimate. If the pay fails our budget, I'll keep the current paid extrusion job while looking for a better offer.

A **paid maintenance route** needs real machine assessment and union support.

Training while employed can protect the **mortgage income** if a real place opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 could handle orders, and capable robots around 2039 could run the physical extrusion line. I'd tell the union we should settle paid training and stop rights before a robot enters the hot end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when those robots arrive. My children will be older, but I cannot assume the mortgage or our costs disappear. Ten years of typical pay could build our reserve if shifts hold; I expect to work beyond 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the paid line work and add fresh money from each full wage after bills. I'll enrol in a paid recognized maintenance course if the factory offers an actual guarded place, then check posted local roles each year. If robotics later cuts my shifts, I'll apply after qualifying only to safe local postings with sufficient regular pay; I'll support the union's request for paid stop-control practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant line change while our own wages look secure today. A decade lets me wait for proved equipment and learn without guessing which job will exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot trial look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first robot trial should run with a cooled die, a clear guard and someone who can stop the conveyor. I'd inspect the first rubber strip for bubbles before anyone raises the speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the union agreement secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union agreement should name paid practice hours and who has stop authority. If the factory will not offer a paid maintenance place, I won't count maintenance pay in our budget.

A decade can grow the **four-month reserve** if full paid shifts continue.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could run my extrusion tasks while the mortgage still needs my wage. A written crew timetable, offered paid guarded maintenance training and a real safe local job at enough pay would give us a route.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: What else should I have asked?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is allowed to stop the hot extrusion line when a robot's die setting makes a bad strip. A clean screen cannot seal a window with bubbled rubber.

headlineQuote: A clean screen cannot seal a window with bubbled rubber.
portrait: **Marco**, 43, is a junior rubber-extrusion operator with secondary school education and typical factory pay.
He and his home-care partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with about four months saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for fault words and waits for proved safe controls before learning new systems.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about wages; he seeks conditional paid maintenance training and real local work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable extrusion robots around 2031 before he can protect the mortgage wage.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan**, offered paid guarded training and posted safe local work at sufficient pay would help.
